Abstract. Geometrically patterned natural interfaces, such as sutures, play a central role in load 11

transfer, enhancing strength, energy, dissipation, while preventing catastrophic failure including 12

woodpecker’s beak, human skull, and turtle shells. These enhanced properties are governed by 13

mechanisms including interlocking, stretching, and pull-out. Inspired by biological toughening 14

strategies, we introduce a soft-hard suture composite assembly for engineering the interlocking 15

and pull-out mechanisms that govern toughness, strength, and ductility. Soft material width (w), 16

along with suture lock angle (θ) is used to understand and design interfaces with high energy 17

dissipation (toughness) and load transfer (strength) capacity. Experiments demonstrate that 18

incorporating soft hyperelastic material between interlocking hard cement paste tablets 19

increasingly produce two distinctive toughening mechanisms (interfacial debonding and ductile 20

pull-out) corresponding to a unique dual-peak response. The hard-soft composite suture 21

assemblies achieve up to 48.3-fold enhancement in toughness and 2.5-fold increase in tensile 22

strength, compared to monolithic (hard-hard) suture counterparts, while preventing brittle 23

failure in hard-phase. Additionally, by engineering the soft materials width (w) together with 24

lock angle (θ), a delayed brittle failure transforms into a ductile pull-out (i.e., no failure). 25

Numerical simulations validate the role of interfacial cohesive properties and softening law in 26

enabling interfacial debonding as a key toughening mechanism. 27

Keywords. Architected materials, Cementitious composites, Bio-inspired interface, Suture, 28

Introduction 40

Nature offers clever designs of materials and interfaces, particularly in overcoming the mutual 41

exclusivity in certain mechanical properties such as toughness and strength.1,2 Unlike 42

conventional engineering materials, which often rely on single-constituents that can suffer from 43

inherent property limitations, biological systems utilize an assembly of dissimilar materials to 44

achieve outstanding mechanical performance.3 For instance, natural materials, such as Mollusk 45

shells and enamel, combine hard minerals (e.g., aragonite, hydroxyapatite) with soft organic 46

constituents (e.g., proteins, collagen) to develop structures that exhibit enhanced toughness, and 47

structural integrity in which interfaces play a crucial role in maintaining mechanical 48

functionality.4–7 49

One of the purposeful strategies in designs of interfaces in nature is the use of interlocking 50

geometries, such as suture-like architectures.8 These interlocking interfaces have evolved to 51

help integrate dissimilar natural materials, playing a crucial role in dissipating energy and 52

enhancing toughness.1,9 Woodpecker’s beak,10 Phloeodes diabolicus's elytra,9 human’s skull,11 53

and turtle’s shell12 are canonical examples for which these architected interfaces are 54

instrumental in controlling crack propagation and energy absorption in biological materials. 55

More specifically, as shown in Figure 1B, the woodpecker’s beak features interlocked suture- 56

like interfaces with a small gap between mineralized tablets, enabling local shearing and 57

promoting energy absorption capacity with enhanced toughness under impact.10,13 In Phloeodes 58

diabolicus, a medial interlocked suture joins the two adjacent elytra, providing high impact, 59

crush and bending resistance.9 Human skull and turtle shell, on the other hand, use interdigitated 60

sutures between hard bones by incorporating a soft tissue at the interface between them (Figure 61

1C,D), with enhanced ductility and impact resistance.11 62

Studies on suture-like engineering interfaces have been carried out on both interlocking and 63

non-interlocking geometries. Specifically, analytical and computational studies have revealed 64

how the suture-like interface geometry (i.e., shape, lock angle) can promote strength, stiffness, 65

and toughness in engineering materials.14–16 A study analyzed four types of suture geometries, 66

namely triangular, rectangular, trapezoidal, and anti-trapezoidal, using an analytical model 67

based on the principle of virtual work. Results showed that anti-trapezoidal patterns exhibit 68

promising strength and toughness, with enhanced damage tolerance due to increased strain to 69

failure and mechanical interlocking.16 70

Previous studies on engineered interlocking systems predominantly focused on hard-hard 71

designs, where both components are considered rigid.17 Additionally, the effectiveness of 72

proposed bistable interlock concepts, particularly in achieving adequate energy dissipation, 73

strongly depends on the strain-hardening behavior of the interlocking components, which limits 74

their application primarily to high-performance cementitious materials.18,19 In contrast, 75

relatively little attention has been devoted to hard-soft interlocking systems, commonly found 76

in natural systems, where a compliant material interlocks with the stiffer counterparts. This 77

distinction is critical, as the mechanical response of hard-soft systems differs fundamentally 78

from that of hard-hard interlocks.5 Therefore, a significant gap remains in the study of 79

engineered suture-like structures that strategically incorporate hard-soft composites.14,15,20 80

In this study, we propose the introduction of a soft hyperelastic interlayer within a suture-like 81

interlocking mechanism to enhance toughness and improve the overall load-bearing capacity of 82

the hard cementitious materials. Specifically, this design strategy enables us to overcome the 83

traditionally mutual exclusivity between toughness and strength, achieving remarkable 84

3

improvements in toughness without sacrificing strength. By developing hard-hard suture-like 85

interfaces (Figure 1E) through engineering key geometric features, specifically the locking 86

angle, we hypothesize to dissipate more energy and enhance toughness. Additionally, by 87

engineering hard-soft suture-like interfaces (Figure 1F) through tailoring geometric features 88

and characteristics of the interlayer, specifically lock angle and thickness, we hypothesize to 89

enhance the toughness, ductility, and tensile strength of composite suture interfaces, surpassing 90

the performance of the benchmark hard-hard suture-like interface (monolithic). 91

We anticipate that the integration of a soft interlayer within the interlocking suture-like 102

architecture can provide additional energy dissipation through two key mechanisms: (1) 103

debonding at the interface between dissimilar materials and (2) pull-out of interlocking tablets. 104

By harnessing the synergy between hard and soft materials through suture-like interfaces, the 105

proposed approach can enable the development of engineered composite assemblies that 106

achieve a unique combination of high strength and toughness. These mechanisms collectively 107

improve mechanical resilience by suppressing brittle failure and preventing catastrophic 108

fracture of the hard phases, thereby opening new pathways for modular, damage-tolerant 109

structural materials. 110

Strength and Ductility 112

Three distinct failure mechanisms are observed in the interlocking monolithic and composite 113

suture interfaces subjected to uniaxial tension (Figure 2A). In benchmark monolithic suture 114

cases, an abrupt brittle failure mode, corresponding to the tensile strength of the cement paste, 115

take place, where the cracks initiate and propagate predominantly in the neck region and/or 116

through the bulk of the suture tablets (Figure 2B mode i, and Supplementary Videos 1, 4, and 7 117

in Supplementary Information). 118

Conversely, the composite suture cases incorporating a PVS interlayer using the same 119

geometric design, exhibit two new failure  modes, namely delayed brittle failure (Figure 2B 120

mode ii, and Supplementary Videos 5, 8, and 9 in Supplementary Information) or ductile failure 121

(Figure 2B mode iii, and Supplementary 2, 3, and 6 in Supplementary Information), both of 122

which represent a novel dual-peak mechanical response for an engineered suture interface under 123

tension. 124

Two additional failure mechanisms in composite suture, namely debonding-tablet in mode ii 125

and debonding-pull out in mode iii, indicate the ability to maintain the tensile strength while 126

enhancing the overall energy absorption and ductility compared to monolithic suture. The 127

occurrence of debonding-tablet failure vs. debonding-pull out failure is dependent upon the 128

geometric parameters, namely the lock angle of the suture blade (θ) and the interlayer gap width 129

(w) (Figure 2F). 130

In particular, in the debonding-tablet failure mechanism  (Figure 2B mode ii), the first peak in 131

the stress-strain response arises due to debonding between the cement paste and PVS, 132

accompanied by a reduction in load-bearing capacity, as shown in Figure 2A (in red dashed 133

line). Continued tensile loading demonstrates a secondary increase in load-bearing capacity, 134

which we hypothesize to emerge from the activation of the mechanical interlocking of the 135

composite suture blades (we later corroborate it numerically). As the applied load further 136

increases and reaches the tensile strength of the cement paste, a brittle tablet failure proceeds 137

(neck and/or bottom side of cement paste tablet), leading to a sharp drop in load and ultimate 138

brittle failure (Figure 2B mode ii). The delayed brittle failure mode is activated by incorporating 139

soft materials into a suture composite interface, facilitating additional load-bearing capacity. 140

In the debonding-pull-out mode (Figure 2B mode iii), a response similar to that of the 141

debonding-tablet failure mode is observed in the initial stages, including debonding of the PVS 142

accompanied by a reduction in load-bearing capacity, and a secondary increase due to the 143

activation of mechanical interlocking between the composite suture blade assembly. However, 144

as shown by the blue dotted line in Figure 2A, the interlocking mechanism here subsequently 145

allows the blades to disengage and gracefully pull out without any brittle failure of the cement 146

matrix tablet. Such ductile failure mode can be tailored by engineering a higher θ and/or a lower 147

w, facilitating higher load-bearing and enhanced energy dissipation while preventing abrupt 148

fracture, without significantly compromising tensile strength. This mode, is thereby, anticipated 149

to offer a desirable interfacial mechanical response compared with mode ii composite and mode 150

I in monolithic suture interfaces. 151

The tensile strength is evaluated for both monolithic and composite suture interface assemblies 152

(Figure 2C), which include variations in θ and w. The studied composite sutures have three 153

different w, namely 1 mm, 2 mm, and 3 mm, and θ ranging from 10° to 45° by 5° increments, 154

with three replicates for each combination (Figure S1). The tensile strength for the monolithic 155

The two distinct strain values at failure are also evaluated for the studied suture interfaces 172

(Figure 2D). These two values are the strain corresponding to PVS debonding and, if present, a 173

second peak associated with the fracture of the cement paste tablets. Except for the monolithic 174

suture interface with θ = 10, which exhibits a pull-out mechanism, all other monolithic suture 175

interfaces exhibit abrupt brittle failure; thus, only a single strain value is reported, 176

corresponding to cement paste failure, with an average of 0.21 ± 0.02%. In contrast, the 177

incorporation of PVS interlayer composite interfaces demonstrates significantly higher strain- 178

at-failure values (i.e., ductility) compared to the monolithic case (Figure 2D). The significantly 179

enhanced ductility of the composite suture interface compared to monolithic suture interfaces 180

is further promoted by increasing w. Considering the strain at first peak associated with PVS 181

debonding among the three composite cases of varying interlayer thickness, no statistically 182

significant differences in ductility were found (ranging from 0.60 ± 0.15% to 1.05 ± 0.27%) as 183

illustrated in Figure 2D. However, considering the strain at the second peak associated with 184

ultimate brittle tablet failure or graceful pull-out among the three composite cases, a significant 185

increase in ductility from 1.37 ± 0.68% to 3.19 ± 1.33% and to 3.22 ± 1.21%, with increasing 186

PVS thickness from 1 mm to 2 and 3 mm. Compared to the monolithic interfaces, the strain at 187

failure in composite sutures is up to 15.5 times higher, indicating significantly enhanced 188

ductility while enhancing the strength. 189

While Figure 2C and Figure 2D represent the average macroscopic strength and ductility 190

properties of the monolithic vs composite interfaces, the specific impact of suture features (θ 191

and w) on the strain-at-failure is further studied. Figure 2E presents the results for the suture 192

composite with w =1mm. In this comparison, the strain at the second peak is primarily 193

considered, as all failures in these samples were classified as delayed brittle failures. 194

Supplementary Figures S5A and Figures S5B show the results for the suture composites with 195

w=2 mm and w=3 mm, respectively. In these cases, either pull-out or delayed brittle failure 196

modes were observed. Given this, the strain at the first peak is used for samples exhibiting pull- 197

out failure (indicated by hatched bars), while for samples with delayed brittle failure, the strain 198

at the second peak is considered. Overall, increasing the θ  enhances interlocking, limiting 199

suture blade displacement and thus reducing strain-at-failure across all three composite groups 200

(w=1-3 mm). 201

Toughness 202

The toughness of monolithic vs. composite suture interface assemblies is examined, quantified 203

using work-of-failure (WOF), defined as the area under the load-displacement curve. Up to four 204

toughening mechanisms in the composite suture, corresponding to elastic stretching, 205

debonding, interlocking, and pull-out can be in play, contributing to the overall toughness of 206

the composite in a unique dual-peak mechanical response (Figure 3A, B). This is in contrast to 207

the monolithic cases where only elastic deformation and a single peak is present prior to failure. 208

dissipative area contributions to toughness corresponding to the mode i and mode ii in the 210

proposed composites, respectively. While the gray area under the curve represents elastic 211

deformation, the yellow area corresponds to strain-softening upon debonding after the first 212

*Figure 3C illustrates the toughness values for the benchmark monolithic suture interfaces with 216*

no soft interlayer. A limited (weak) interlocking and pull-out between the two cement paste 217

tablets can be present, only at a low θ =10°, without a brittle fracture of the cement paste tablets. 218

However, this interlocking leads to a very small amount of energy dissipation (7.6 N.mm). As 219

the θ  increases up to 20°, the toughness substantially increases (reaching a maximum value of 220

74 N.mm) due to a greater geometric interlocking, followed by a significant decrease in 221

toughness, hypothesized due to higher stress concentration coupled with narrower w at 222

increasing θ  (i.e., lower peak and strain-at-failure). The substantial interlocking at θ larger than 223

10°, leads to a brittle fracture in the neck and a lack of pull-out (i.e., mode i). 224

In contrast to the monolithic suture interfaces that demonstrate limited toughness (below 80 225

N.mm), more than one order of magnitude higher toughness values are present in composite 226

suture counterparts of the same θ  and w (Figure 3D-F). It is observed that in all composite 227

specimens, increasing the θ  from a low value (e.g., 10°) to a critical threshold (15-30 degrees, 228

which varies depending on the w) leads to a significant increase in toughness due to additional 229

composite mechanisms of energy dissipation (i.e., elastic stretching, debonding, interlocking, 230

and pull-out). 231

Depending on the θ  and w, the WOF ranges from 140 to 1040 N.mm, achieving up to 14 times 232

higher toughness compared to the best-performing monolithic benchmarks (74 N.mm). In 233

addition, a general transition from a ‘delayed brittle failure’ (mode ii) to ‘ductile failure’ (mode 234

iii) is observed, taking place at a critical θ. As the layer thickness increases (Figure 3D,E,F), 235

the critical angle at which the favorable transition occurs increases. It must be noted that for a 236

given w, the transition from a ductile mode iii to a delayed failure mode ii marks an inflection 237

point where the most effective energy dissipation occurs at the largest angle at which mode iii 238

can take place (i.e., at θ = 15, 20, 30, in Figure 3D, E, F, respectively). 239

Among all studied configurations, the composite suture with w=3 mm and θ=30° exhibits the 240

highest WOF, mainly due to the highest interlocking/softening contribution and the substantial 241

energy dissipation during the pull-out. 242

Specifically, points A1 and B1 (Figure 4A, B) correspond to the linear-elastic domain prior to 254

followed by a hardening in the stress-strain response (Figure 4C) in both composite interfaces, 259

attributed to the activation of the interlocking mechanisms, at two distinct slopes. In composite 260

suture with θ = 45° and w = 3 mm, the hardening is followed by a brittle tablet fracture (Figure 261

4C) as highlighted in A3 (Figure 4A), characteristic of the mode ii failure. On the other hand, in 262

composite suture with θ = 30°, w = 3 mm, the hardening is followed by a graceful softening 263

(Figure 4C) instead of a brittle fracture as demonstrated in B3 (Figure 4B), characteristic of the 264

mode iii failure. 265

The two distinct behaviors highlight how a dual-peak response can be engineered into 266

composite (hard-soft) interfaces. Specifically, incorporation of a soft interlayer into monolithic 267

(hard-hard) interfaces and engineering the geometric features (i.e., θ), further enhance the load- 268

bearing capacity, ductility, and energy dissipation/toughening while preventing brittle failure. 269

More specifically, engineering mode iii failure corresponds to a dual-peak response with two 270

graceful softening due to debonding and pull-out. Design of composite hard-soft interface 271

assemblies using this failure mechanism is desirable in which a more gradual, non-brittle 272

response, in contrast to the more abrupt failure in monolithic counterparts, can be achieved 273

while both the strength (by 2.2-fold) and toughness (by 15.5-fold) of the interface is 274

significantly improved. 275

Discussion 283

In the monolithic  suture system, we observe that failure initiates and propagates abruptly once 284

the tensile strength of the cement paste is exceeded, leading to a catastrophic fracture mode 285


<!-- Page 12 -->


11

(Figure 2B.I). This behavior is characteristic of brittle materials, where failure is localized and 286

energy dissipation is minimal. Such brittle failure is eliminated by introducing a soft interlayer 287

into an interlocking suture mechanism and enabling a dual-peak graceful deformation. 288

Specifically, composite sutures with a PVS interlayer exhibit substantially enhanced toughness, 289

as evidenced by significant increases in both strain at failure and WOF (Figure 3C-E). These 290

improvements are driven by the sequential activation of toughening mechanisms, including 291

interfacial debonding, mechanical interlocking, and ultimately ductile pull-out, each dependent 292

on the specific geometry. Considering the parametric study on geometric features of the 293

composites suture interface, namely lock angle (θ) and interlayer width (w), we reveal that a 294

lower θ and a larger w promotes ductile pull-out (mode iii) over delayed brittle failure (mode 295

ii) (Figure 2B). 296

This study further investigates the impact of suture blade number on the mechanical 297

performance of the composite suture interface assembly with a locking angle of 30° and w=3 298

mm. As shown in Figure S2A, the initial peak force, associated with PVS debonding, does not 299

change across single-, double-, and triple-blade configurations. However, the post-peak 300

response differs significantly, with multi-blade samples showing step-wise cracking due to 301

increased interlocking interfaces. This helps delay the onset of brittle failure and enhance 302

energy dissipation. Specifically, we observe that the WOF increases significantly from 1008 ± 303

422 to 2135 ± 92 N.mm as the suture blade count increases from one to three (Figure S2B). A 304

comparison of the WOF across four interface types, namely single monolithic suture, composite 305

flat, single composite suture assembly, and triple composite suture assembly, demonstrates how 306

leveraging hard-soft composites in combination with bio-inspired suture patterns can enhance 307

toughness by up to 85 times (Figure S3). 308

The  superior performance of the proposed engineered composite suture assemblies collectively, 309

in terms of toughness and strength is further highlighted in the Ashby plot (Figure 5), where 310

they are benchmarked against the collective monolithic suture and the bulk properties of similar 311

classes of materials (i.e., cement paste, mortar, concrete, fiber-reinforced concrete, strain- 312

hardening cementitious composites, and polymers). This comparison with bulk material 313

properties serves to contextualize the mechanical compatibility of the proposed composite 314

sutures with conventional cement-based materials. Such compatibility may be relevant for the 315

integration of these hard-soft suture interfaces into modular structural systems that utilize these 316

bulk cementitious materials. Specifically, the engineered composite sutures outperform the 317

cement paste class of material by nearly an order of magnitude in toughness (Figure 5). 318

Specifically, the single-blade composite suture achieves a tensile strength of 0.2 MPa and a 319

WOF of 12.23 kJ/m³, corresponding to 1.3-fold and 33.6-fold improvements, respectively, over 320

monolithic sutures. Furthermore, increasing the number of suture blades while maintaining the 321

same geometric and interlayer parameters enhances both strength and toughness even further 322

up to 2.5-fold and 48.3-fold, respectively. These results underscore the efficacy of geometrically 323

engineered, bio-inspired interfaces in elevating the toughness of brittle materials to levels 324

approaching or surpassing those of high-performance composites. 325

Numerical evaluation of interfacial debonding mechanism and global vs. interfacial 331

response 332

To further understand and interpret the experimentally observed response of the composite 333

suture assemblies, uniaxial tension simulations (under the same loading conditions as the 334

experiments) for the case with a PVS with w=3 mm was performed. The material properties 335

used in the model for both bulk elements (i.e., hardened cement paste and PVS) and interface 336

(i.e., PVS-hardened cement paste interface) were obtained from tensile and fracture 337

characterization described in the Experimental section. The numerical simulations were carried 338

out using a recently developed framework 21 for hard-soft architected materials that couple 339

large-deformation solid mechanics with phase-field fracture in the bulk and cohesive zone 340

modeling (CZM) along the hard-soft interface, implemented as a user element (UEL) for use in 341

Abaqus. 22,23 342

*Figure 6A demonstrates that increasing the θ from 15° to 45° increases the first peak load 343*

attained during the initial loading stage that results in debonding, similar to the experimental 344

findings. The accompanying field quantities at the peak load in Figure 6B-D (corresponding to 345


<!-- Page 14 -->


13

the points marked by a square and I, II, III in Figure 6A) reveal the mechanical origin of this 346

trend and the underlying trade-off in relation to θ for a constant w. The results highlight that 347

bulk normal stress component (S22) becomes progressively concentrated near the interlock neck 348

region as the θ increases (Figure 6B). Specifically, the maximum normal stress component (S22) 349

increases from 0.31 MPa at θ = 15° to 0.83 MPa at θ = 45°, revealing a clear geometric effect 350

(Supplementary Videos 10, 11, and 12 in Supplementary Information). While larger θ improve 351

geometric constraint and therefore increase the macroscopic load that can be transmitted across 352

the suture, they simultaneously amplify local tensile stress within the brittle cementitious phase. 353

This provides a mechanistic explanation for the experimentally observed angle dependence, 354

whereby improved peak load can come at the expense of increased propensity for localization 355

in cementitious phase, leading to a subsequent cracking once the local tensile stress reaches the 356

strength limit of the brittle phase. 357

The shear stress component (S12) also remains strongly localized around the interlocking 358

shoulders and curved transitions (Figure 6C), supporting that load transfer is not purely tensile 359

opening. Instead, the interlocking geometry produces mixed-mode transfer (normal opening 360

combined with shear), which becomes increasingly important, especially once the interface 361

begins to degrade and debond. Consistent with this result, the normal cohesive traction 362

distribution along the PVS-cement interface (Figure 6D) indicates that the interface is the 363

primary location of damage initiation and early energy dissipation in the suture composite, 364

rather than immediate bulk fracture through the cementitious tablets for all small to large θ 365

(Supplementary Videos 13, 14, and 15 in Supplementary). A key point is that the highest 366

interface normal tractions shown in Figure 6D are capped by the cohesive normal strength 367

specified in the model. In this study, the cohesive normal strength was set to 0.19 MPa in the 368

Abaqus input per experimentally characterized properties as shown in the Experimental section. 369

Accordingly, regions that reach this level of normal traction are precisely the regions expected 370

to trigger damage initiation in the CZM element (i.e., the PVS-cement interface). The traction 371

contour, therefore, supports the experimental interpretation that the first peak corresponds to 372

the onset of interfacial debonding. The local regions along the interface reach the prescribed 373

traction threshold first (i.e., cohesive normal strength of 0.19 MPa), where the interfacial 374

damage locally initiates and propagates as shown in the contour of Figure 6D for all angles. 375

The interface therefore degrades progressively, prior to either pull-out without interlocking at 376

𝜃 = 15° or the brittle fracture in the case of 𝜃= 45°. It must be noted that the traction peak is 377

spatially distributed across a broader area of the interface elements at smaller θ (e.g., 15), 378

decreasing with increasing θ, indicating lower stress concentration at smaller θ at the interface 379

area (Figure 6D) consistent with the S22 contours. 380

The post-peak interface response indicative of near-complete loss of traction at the interface 402

(i.e., near-complete debonding), reveals correspondence to a rather significant load drop in the 403

It is worth noting that the simulation reveals the load reduction in the global response can take 406

place at the presence of debonding mechanism between hard and soft materials, without 407

requiring catastrophic failure in the hard cementitious phase. The findings also reveal that the 408

majority of interface softening (taking place from Point II to III), occur near the post-peak 409

region in the global response; a phenomenon that would be evident without a temporal 410

comparison of interfacial and global failure mechanisms. 411

The sequence of snapshots (I-VI) of interface cohesive traction (Figure 7C) clarifies how 412

debonding develops spatially (Suppl Video 14, Supplementary Information). Early in loading 413

(I-II), regions of cohesive strength saturation begin small and broadly extends/distributes across 414

the interface as engaged by the suture. As loading progresses (III-IV), and traction further 415

localizes and debonding begins at the exterior/shoulder of the suture (shown in purple low 416

traction starting at III and at the tip of the suture starting at IV), after which the traction-carrying 417

area rapidly diminishes as the debonded region rapidly grows. At later stages (V-VI), substantial 418

portions of the interface lose traction-carrying capability, consistent with advanced interfacial 419

separation and reduced global load drop. 420

Notably, the bulk normal stress field in the same snapshots demonstrate that once interfacial 421

traction degrades, stress transfer through the bulk hard-soft contact is mostly lost and is instead 422

re-routed into the interlocking geometry (after which, whether it would lead to pull-out, brittle 423

failure, or interlocking dissipation would depend on the θ) (Suppl Video 11, Supplementary 424

Information). This provides the evidence the transition that was inferred experimentally: after 425

debonding initiates, the system does not “lose” load transfer entirely; instead, load is 426

increasingly carried by geometric engagement/contact and progressive pull-out, which sustains 427

The proposed interlocking suture composites can be employed in a wide range of applications, 441

including structural elements such as walls, pavements, and columns, with enhanced 442

mechanical properties and promising toughness. Their compatibility with modular construction 443

approaches allows for prefabricated components with precise interlocking features, facilitating 444

rapid assembly (e.g., with 3D-printing), ease of replacement, and improved construction 445

efficiency. As a result, these composites provide a promising pathway toward more resilient, 446

adaptable, and long-lasting construction materials. 447

Conclusion 448

This work demonstrates that bio-inspired hard-soft composite suture interfaces provide an 449

effective architectural strategy for overcoming the strength-toughness trade-off in cementitious 450

materials. By integrating a compliant interlayer within interlocking suture geometries, 451

substantial enhancements in tensile strength (up to 2.2 times) and toughness (up to 14.1 times) 452

are achieved relative to monolithic suture interfaces, highlighting the governing role of interface 453

architecture in failure control. Tailoring the suture lock angle (θ) and gap width (w) in the 454

presence of a soft interlayer suppresses brittle fracture and activates a dual-peak load- 455

deformation response characteristic of progressive damage and graceful failure, enabling a 456

transition from abrupt brittle cracking to ductile pull-out-dominated failure through sequential 457

interfacial debonding and geometric interlocking. Further gains are realized by increasing the 458

number of suture blades, which promotes step-wise crack propagation and delays catastrophic 459

failure; notably, the three-blade composite suture achieves a work-of-fracture that is 1.6 times 460

and 2.1 times higher than the two-blade and single-blade configurations, respectively. 461

A systematic comparison across monolithic suture, composite flat, single composite suture, and 462

triple composite suture interfaces reveals that combining hard-soft material contrast with bio- 463

inspired suture architecture enhances toughness by up to 85 times, establishing interface 464

tailoring as a powerful design principle for achieving simultaneous strength, toughness, and 465

damage tolerance in advanced structural materials. The improved performance of proposed 466

hard-soft suture assemblies, significantly promoted by energy dissipation at hard-soft 467


<!-- Page 19 -->


18

interfaces, allows for energetically favorable pull-out and a graceful separation without failure 468

(i.e., allowing to recover and re-assemble the interlock). 469

Numerical simulations validate the role of interfacial cohesive properties and cohesive 470

softening law in enabling the interfacial debonding as a key toughening mechanism, 471

highlighting that as interfacial tractions degradation delays the stress transfer to geometric 472

interlocking, where the pull-out, brittle failure, or interlocking-dominated dissipation, 473

depending on θ.  The simulations indicate that, first macroscopic load reduction is driven by 474

interfacial debonding rather than catastrophic hard-phase failure or pull-out. 475

The simulation supports the experimental evidence that debonding is a new toughening 476

mechanism, enabled by introduction of soft materials, which can enhance the fracture 477

toughness, without sacrificing the strength. It demonstrates the interconnection between 478

interfacial separation and macroscopic debonding, that is once interfacial traction moves to 479

softening, stress transfer through the bulk hard-soft contact is mostly lost and is instead re- 480

routed into the interlocking geometry (after which, whether it would lead to pull-out, brittle 481

failure, or interlocking dissipation would depend on the θ). In other words, both experiments 482

and simulations consistently highlight that after debonding initiates, load transfer persists 483

through geometric engagement and progressive pull-out, resulting in a non-zero residual load 484

and continued energy dissipation. 485

Such interlocking structures allow for large deformation while absorbing higher energy and 486

undergoing higher tensile capacities, while delaying catastrophic failure. The proposed hard- 487

soft suture assembly enables engineering tough, ductile, and strong interfaces through a 488

geometric design strategy and helps overcome the otherwise brittle nature of hard-hard 489

interfaces. These assemblies are inherently scalable with significant potential for applications 490

in precast-to-precast and precast-to-in situ concrete connections in slabs and beams, modular 491

wall panels and rapid tilt-up construction,  hull panels in rowboats and sectional structures such 492

as kayaks, hard-soft robotics with limited degrees of freedom and force-control or joints with 493

tailored tensile for transfer capacity. 494

Currently, additive manufacturing of civil infrastructure and energy structures suffer from 495

surface geometric imperfections, limiting the modular construction with additively 496

manufactured sub-components, otherwise requiring subtractive manufacturing. Building on the 497

insight for the small-scale efforts in this study, future work can include incorporating soft 498

materials at the interfaces of additively manufacturing concrete or steel structures, eliminating 499

the need for subtractive manufacturing and allowing for connections with extremely high 500

toughness and ductility under tension, where the hard quasi-brittle concrete or hard-hard 501

concrete suture interlocks have a limited capacity. Thereby, allow for further scaling up of 502

design and construction of modular 3D-printed components at large scale – given the current 503

upper limit in real-world (e.g., housing, offshore components) is limited by the size of the 504

printer and tolerance (i.e., geometric errors) which are otherwise handled through subtractive 505

manufacturing or feedback control methods.24,25 506

Moreover, proposed suture assembly can also allow for construction of large structures such as 507

beams, walls, bridges, and pavement blocks potentially without reinforcement or with minimal 508

reinforcement toward larger scales. 509

Cement Paste Mix Design and Sample Preparation: The cement paste is prepared using a water- 511

to-cement ratio of 0.33 with commercially available Type-I cement from Buzzi Unicem 512

(Stockertown, PA, USA). To enhance workability, a plasticizer (Glenium 7700) is incorporated 513

into the mix at a dosage of 0.4% by mass of the cement. The mixing process follows a two-step 514

procedure26,27. In the first step, the material is pre-mixed for 25 seconds, then mixed at 400 rpm 515

for 90 seconds under 70% vacuum. In the second step, mixing is continued at 400 rpm for 90 516

seconds under full (100%) vacuum. As shown in Figure S3, the suture blade geometry consists 517

of three identical circular shapes. Specifically, seven different θ ranging from 15° to 45° in 5- 518

degree intervals and four different w (0, 1, 2, and 3 mm) are considered (Figure S1). Considering 519

the suture geometric features, the polylactic acid (PLA) models are first 3D printed using the 520

Ultimaker S5 device. All samples have a width of 70 mm and a thickness of 15 mm, 521

respectively. The samples are fabricated in a laboratory environment at a temperature of 23 ± 4 522

°C and a humidity of 49 ± 5%. After fabrication, they are transferred to a sealed chamber 523

maintained at a relative humidity of 95 ± 2% using a saturated potassium sulfate solution.28 The 524

samples are initially cured in the chamber for 24 hours, demolded, and then kept there for an 525

additional six days. 526

Polyvinyl Siloxane (PVS) interlayer: A two-part polyvinyl siloxane (PVS) material, specifically 527

the Elite Double 32 (Zhermack), is selected for this study due to its hyperelastic properties. This 528

PVS has a nominal low viscosity of 3.23 ± 0.08 mPa.s upon mixing and a nominal setting time 529

of 20 minutes at 23 °C. The material is prepared by manually mixing the base and curing agent 530

in a 2:1 weight ratio for 60 seconds under laboratory conditions at a temperature of 23 ± 4 °C 531

and humidity of 49 ± 5%. The low viscosity of the selected PVS makes it suitable for use under 532

these conditions. The fresh PVS is immediately injected into the pre-set gap (w) along the 533

interface using a syringe. The composite samples are then kept in the lab's ambient conditions 534

for seven days before performing the mechanical tests. 535

Mechanical Testing of Bulk Materials: The uniaxial tension test was conducted to characterize 536

the tensile strength and work of failure (WOF) of monolithic and composite suture interfaces. 537

All samples measured 180 ± 5 mm in length, 70 mm in width, and 15 mm in height. 538

Additionally, the tensile properties of the individual bulk materials, PVS and cement paste, were 539

characterized using dog-bone specimens according to ASTM D412-16 and JSCE standards, 540

respectively (Figure S4). 29,30 Tensile tests were conducted on all specimens using an Instron 541

testing machine equipped with tensile grips and serrated jaw faces. A constant crosshead 542

displacement rate of 1 mm/min was used for all suture and bulk cement paste specimens, while 543

bulk PVS specimens were tested at a loading rate of 150 mm/min. 544

Furthermore, the fracture toughness of PVS was measured using the tear (trouser) test, with 545

specimens consisting of a rectangular strip (width 15 mm, length 150 mm, thickness ݐ௦ = 2 mm) 546

with a longitudinal pre-cut (notch) of 40 mm in accordance with ASTM-D624 31. The cut 547

specimens were then clamped into MTS Criterion C45.305 and pulled at a constant 548

displacement rate of 50 mm/min. The fracture toughness (ܩ௖ ௣) was calculated as ܩ௖ ௣= 2ܨ௔௩௚/ݐ௦ 549

where ܨ௔௩௚ is the average tearing force in the plateau region and ݐ௦ is the sample thickness. To 550

prevent crack path deflection toward specimen edges, the sides of the specimen were reinforced 551

with Kapton polyimide tape, whose stiffness is negligible. Elastomer sheets were cast in molds 552

and cured for 7 days before cutting. Specimens were tested at room temperature, and the point 553

Mechanical Testing of Interfacial Properties: 566

The interfacial cohesive properties between hardened cement paste and PVS were determined 567

as follows. The tensile cohesive strength (normal cohesive traction) and Mode I fracture 568

toughness were determined using single-edge notch test in uniaxial tension. Specimen geometry 569

consisted of two hardened cement paste blocks with a 1-mm thick PVS layer placed in between, 570

each having a length of 50 mm, width of 25 mm and thickness of 6 mm (Figure S6A). A small 571

notch measuring 5 mm was introduced at the interface between the two materials and direct 572

tension tests were performed at a displacement rate of 0.02 mm/min until full separation. The 573

peak stress taken as the cohesive normal traction, and the area under the traction-separation 574

curve was taken as the Mode I fracture toughness. The tangential cohesive strength was 575

obtained using the asymmetric four-point bend test.33 A 1-mm thick layer was inserted between 576

two rectangular prisms of cement paste, each with dimensions of 40 mm × 20 mm × 20 mm. 577

The PVS was sandwiched to the face of the prisms with the dimension of 20 mm × 20 mm. The 578

positioning of the upper and lower rollers was asymmetric, ensuring the PVS-cement paste 579

interface was aligned with the center load-line (ASTM C1469-22, 2022). The tests were 580

performed at a displacement rate of 0.02 mm/min until failure of the interface on one side 581

between the cement paste and the PVS layer was observed. Lastly, Mode II fracture toughness 582

was determined using the Brazil-nut test (Figure S6B). 34 This test involved placing a 1-mm 583

thin layer between two semi-cylindrical pieces of cement paste to form a cylindrical sample 584

with a diameter of 50 mm, a thickness of 12 mm, a notch length of 16.3 mm (equivalent to one- 585

third of the diameter), and a notch width of 7 mm. The Brazil-Nut test facilitates the control of 586

the fracture mode by adjusting the diametral compression angle, 𝜃. For Mode II setting, 𝜃 is 587

equal to 27.2°. 35 The load was applied at the displacement rate of 0.05 mm/min until failure of 588

the interface on one side between the cement paste and PVS layer was achieved. 589

In all tests, three replicates are considered and the data are presented as mean ± standard 590

deviation (SD). For statistical analysis, a one-tailed F-test is used to assess differences in 591

variance, and a T-test is used to compare means, both with a 95% confidence interval. An alpha 592

value of 0.05 is considered the threshold for statistical significance, where p < 0.05 indicates a 593

significant difference between samples. Each test is performed with a minimum of two 594

repetitions. Statistical analysis is conducted using the Data Analysis Toolpak in Microsoft 595

Excel. 596
